**Treatment of earlier authority:** Hansberry requires genuine adequate representation. Matsushita preserves that prerequisite apart from notice and opt-out rights; Richards rejects a shared objective as a substitute, and Shutts's separate safeguards do not cure the conflict.

##### IV. Individual claims and governing-law differences defeat predominance

**Independent alternative holding:** The proposed class also fails Rule 23(b)(3) because its common asbestos-exposure and settlement objectives do not predominate over the materially different state laws, exposure histories, causation, injuries, defenses and individual claims. Removing trial-management concerns does not remove those substantive differences.

**Proposition-level authority for alternative holding:** Part IV has the same six-Justice coalition as Part III and independently supports affirmance. Stevens and Breyer withhold this application as well.

**Material application:** Differences include product identification, latency, limitations, defenses, damages and applicable state law. A shared payment compromise does not establish that common substantive questions predominate.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Nationwide, mass-tort, issue and settlement classes are not categorically prohibited. No particular state-law claim or revised settlement is adjudicated; Metro-North's FELA holding does not establish the validity or injury status of these state-law claims.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Adequacy and predominance are independently sufficient grounds for affirmance, 6–2, leaving certification, settlement approval and the classwide injunction vacated. O'Connor does not participate. No new subclasses, compensation, approval or individual damages ruling is ordered.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Castano's governing-law and proof inquiry and Falcon's actual-prerequisite rule apply despite elimination of trial-management issues. Rhone-Poulenc retains distinct extraordinary-writ limits, and Adams supplies no settlement merits ruling.

### Review and authority of consent decrees

#### Lawyer v. Department of Justice

**Docket or dockets:** No. 95-2024.

**Decided:** 1997-06-25.

For the governing-law error and confined remand of the districting decree, see Lawyer v. Department of Justice, No. 95-2024, decided 1997-06-25, Election Law — Districting consent decrees and preserved claims.

##### I. The personal challenge to this decree remains reviewable

**Holding:** A voter with an established personal relationship to the challenged electoral assignment and decree may obtain review of the decree and the disposition of his own claims even when his design-only constitutional theory fails. This three-judge court's grant of districting injunctive relief is directly reviewable under 28 U.S.C. §§2284 and 1253; neither receipt of part of the requested practical relief nor failure on that substantive theory eliminates the controversy.

**Proposition-level authority:** Breyer's signed Opinion of the Court, Parts I–IV, is joined in full by Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg. Eight Justices directly support every rule and qualification below. The opinion applies the existing Shaw, Miller and Vera rule as governing law; it does not attribute renewed substantive endorsement of that rule to O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy or Thomas. No combination of separate writings or narrowest-ground inference supplies the Court's authority.

**Limits and questions not reached:** This is no general resident-standing rule. The Court orders no Article III, mootness or insubstantiality dismissal.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Miller and Vera separate personal electoral assignment from substantive success and support direct review. Lujan retains personal injury, causation and redressability; Goosby's narrow insubstantiality exception does not convert this merits failure into jurisdictional dismissal.

##### II. General consent authority does not settle every districting-authority objection

**Holding:** A lawful consent decree may impose obligations broader than the relief obtainable after a trial without invariably requiring a prior adjudication of liability, but it must resolve a dispute within subject-matter jurisdiction, remain within the pleadings' general scope, advance the underlying law's objectives and comply with law. One litigant cannot veto the other parties' lawful settlement merely by withholding consent; their agreement nevertheless cannot extinguish his properly raised valid claim or impose duties on him without consent.

**Proposition-level authority:** Breyer's signed Opinion of the Court, Parts I–IV, is joined in full by Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg. Eight Justices directly support every rule and qualification below. The opinion applies the existing Shaw, Miller and Vera rule as governing law; it does not attribute renewed substantive endorsement of that rule to O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy or Thomas. No combination of separate writings or narrowest-ground inference supplies the Court's authority.

**Material application:** Authorized litigation representatives made a genuine state settlement choice, but the March 19, 1996 judicial decree gave Plan 386 compulsory force. No legislative joint resolution or superseding state judgment adopting it is established.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court does not decide whether every federal districting decree needs an established violation or whether authorized litigation settlement always satisfies the State's redistricting opportunity. Neither four-Justice concurrence's additional position controls, and Stone's dissent supplies no fifth judgment-supporting vote for either.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Firefighters applies with its jurisdiction, pleading-scope, underlying-law, legality and nonconsenter conditions; its general settlement latitude does not decide all reapportionment objections. Growe requires respect for actual timely state action, without converting a proposal into enactment. Richards and Matsushita distinguish opportunity to object from lawful authority over retained rights.

### Electoral informational injury and statutory review

#### Akins v. FEC

**Docket or dockets:** D.C. Circuit No. 94-5088; no separate Supreme Court docket supplied.

**Decided:** 1997-06-25.

For political-committee coverage and the separate membership and transaction provisions, see Akins v. FEC, D.C. Circuit No. 94-5088, decided 1997-06-25, Election Law — Political-committee coverage and membership communications.

##### I. The continuing denial of particular electoral information is a concrete injury

**Holding:** Voters denied particular campaign-financing information allegedly required by FECA, which they seek for their own electoral participation, have a concrete informational injury even when many voters share it. Here the Commission's legal ground blocks a statutory process capable of supplying information still sought; the possibility of a later lawful discretionary choice does not defeat traceability or redressability.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part I of Souter's Court opinion is joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Ginsburg and Breyer: seven direct votes.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Statutory complainant status, opposition to an organization's policies or a generalized wish for legal compliance alone is insufficient. The plaintiffs must support their own injury at the litigation stage; standing determines neither entitlement to every requested item nor ultimate regulatory classification.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Public Citizen supports a concrete widely shared informational injury. Lujan retains personal injury and stage-appropriate proof. Bennett requires examination of the real remedial chain despite lawful discretion. Steel Co.'s completed deprivation and already-current reports are distinguished from information still withheld.

##### II. FECA permits review of this dismissal's legal premise

**Holding:** Section 437g(a)(8) permits an aggrieved complainant to obtain judicial review of a complaint dismissal within sixty days and permits correction of a legally erroneous coverage premise. A court may declare the dismissal contrary to law and may direct conformity within thirty days; if the Commission fails to conform, the complainant may bring an action to remedy the violation involved in the original complaint.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part II has the same seven-Justice coalition as Part I.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The separate 120-day inaction route is not invoked. Judicial correction does not compel prosecution, disclosure or penalties, remove lawful discretion, or permit substitution of the agency's separate corporate-prohibition membership rationale for the actual political-committee dismissal ground. Genuine ambiguity and remaining discretion remain for lawful agency consideration.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Standing and legal-error review are affirmed, 7–2; the case returns through the enacted review channel. The separate corporate-prohibition nonenforcement choice is not disturbed merely by correcting this dismissal.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Brown Group separates statutory enforcement authority from Article III. Bennett requires an actual authorized channel, and Legi-Tech preserves lawful agency reconsideration and statutory prerequisites. The agency's interpretation of constitutional decisions is not conclusive because it administers FECA.

### Legislator standing

#### Raines v. Byrd

**Docket or dockets:** No. 96-1671.

**Decided:** June 26, 1997.

##### Whether individual Members may challenge abstract institutional dilution after fully effective votes

**Holding:** Individual Members of Congress whose votes were counted and given full effect lack Article III standing to challenge the Line Item Veto Act on the asserted abstract dilution of Congress's institutional power and alteration of future votes. Express statutory permission to sue removes the applicable prudential obstacle but cannot supply the missing concrete personal injury.

**Proposition-level authority:** Scalia's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Kennedy, Thomas and Ginsburg; six direct rationale votes. Souter supplies the seventh judgment vote on a separate ground.

**Material application:** The Members lost votes that were counted and identify no personal injury from a cancellation; neither House authorized them to represent Congress.

**Limits and questions not reached:** No categorical bar to legislator or official injury is established. Personal exclusion, lost salary, nullified decisive votes, an authorized institutional claim satisfying Article III and concrete cancellation injury remain distinct. Legislative remedies create no exhaustion requirement; no independent traceability holding is added.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Lujan supplies concrete personal injury, without enlargement of its noncontrolling redressability analysis. Akins's concrete shared informational injury is distinguished. Powell preserves personal exclusion claims; Coleman preserves complete nullification of decisive votes. Bender and Allen support the personal-stake and unauthorized-representation boundaries.

##### What disposition follows from the Members' lack of standing

**Holding:** Because these plaintiffs lack Article III standing, the District Court's constitutional declaration must be vacated and the complaint dismissed for lack of jurisdiction. The Court does not decide the Act's constitutionality, nondelegation, Presentment or the independent ripeness question.

**Proposition-level authority:** Scalia's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Kennedy, Thomas and Ginsburg; six direct rationale votes. Souter supplies the seventh judgment vote on a separate ground.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Vacate the District Court's constitutional declaration and remand for jurisdictional dismissal, 7–2. Vacatur neither sustains the Act nor orders a merits remand.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Steel Co. requires resolution of disputed Article III power before disputed merits in this setting; statutory expedition and direct review do not supply constitutional injury.

### Direct appeals and superseding final judgments

#### Foreman v. Dallas County

**Docket or dockets:** Nos. 96-987 and 96-1389.

**Decided:** June 27, 1997.

For the coverage, submission and baseline holdings in Foreman v. Dallas County, June 27, 1997, Nos. 96-987 and 96-1389, see Election Law — Voting Rights Act preclearance.

##### Whether the final dismissal supersedes the earlier injunction appeal under §1253

**Holding:** A qualifying interlocutory refusal of an injunction is appealable under 28 U.S.C. §1253, but the subsequent final dismissal absorbs the same prospective-relief dispute presented here. No. 96-987 is dismissed on that ground; the final judgment remains reviewable in No. 96-1389.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part I of the per curiam opinion, joined by Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer; eight votes. Stone-Zsela concurs only in this judgment.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court establishes no universal finality requirement and does not reclassify the earlier order as a temporary restraining order.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Dismiss No. 96-987 unanimously; final-judgment review proceeds in No. 96-1389.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Shaffer v. Carter supplies merger where a final decree encompasses the same injunction dispute; the statutory interlocutory route remains available.

### Official injury and statutory commands

#### Printz v. United States; Mack v. United States

**Docket or dockets:** Nos. 95-1478 and 95-1503.

**Decided:** June 27, 1997.

**Companion or consolidated matters:** The consolidated Printz and Mack dockets receive the same confined constitutional disposition.

For the limited executive-assistance rule and the fractured fiscal mandate in Printz/Mack, June 27, 1997, Nos. 95-1478 and 95-1503, see Constitutional Structure — Temporary state executive assistance.

##### Whether the plaintiff officers may challenge duties imposed on their offices

**Holding:** A federal command requiring these plaintiff officers to perform identified work through their offices presents a concrete injury redressable by relief against that command. Their official status does not bar review, but it supplies no standing to obtain an advisory decision about independent obligations imposed only on absent dealers or purchasers.

**Proposition-level authority:** Jurisdictional section of Souter's opinion, unanimous.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Government's disavowal of criminal prosecution does not remove the compulsory civil work. Separate criminal-vagueness, unraised civil-vagueness and Thirteenth Amendment matters outside the grant remain undisturbed.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Raines's unauthorized institutional dilution is distinguished from duties imposed directly on the challengers; no universal bar to official injury or standing for absent parties follows.

### Domestic-relations boundaries

#### United States v. Mussari; United States v. Schroeder

**Docket or dockets:** Ninth Circuit Nos. 95-10479 and 95-10513; district cases CR-95-00009-PGR and CR-95-00010-1-PGR. No separate Supreme Court docket number is supplied.

**Decided:** June 30, 1997.

For the interstate-payment and private-regulation holdings in Mussari/Schroeder, June 30, 1997, Ninth Circuit Nos. 95-10479 and 95-10513, see Constitutional Structure — Interstate support-payment obligations. For the offense-date and restitution limits, see Criminal Procedure — Interstate support offenses and temporal limits.

##### Whether the domestic-relations exception bars these federal criminal prosecutions

**Holding:** The limited domestic-relations exception does not bar §228 prosecutions enforcing an existing operative support order. Federal courts may decide offense elements and lawful defenses but may not create or modify support, custody, parentage or domestic status.

**Proposition-level authority:** Opinion of the Court (O'Connor), Parts I–IV, unanimous.

**Limits and questions not reached:** A cognizable challenge to the existence or continued operation of the predicate order is preserved. Hypothetical interference with a different state proceeding is not decided.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Ankenbrandt confines the statutory diversity exception to issuing divorce, alimony and child-custody decrees; it creates no general Article III exclusion of family-related disputes.

## Standards and Tests selection: Intermediary contribution limits and meaningful association

### Intermediary contribution limits and meaningful association

**Governing question:** Fit of limits on contributions received by political committees and political funds.

**Current rule:** Contributions remain distinct from independent expenditures. A broadly restrictive ceiling on contributions received by political committees or funds must preserve meaningful collective political association and fit an identified corruption or circumvention mechanism. Realistic routes around valid candidate limits may be regulated; an insufficiently fitted ceiling cannot be sustained merely by invoking circumvention. The invalidation of the reviewed $100 aggregate annual ceiling establishes no permanent constitutional dollar minimum.

**Authority by component:**

- This $100 intermediary-contribution ceiling lacks sufficient fit: This $100 intermediary-contribution ceiling lacks sufficient fit, 1995-05-15. Stone-Zsela's Opinion of the Court, Part III, joined by Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer: nine direct votes, at this stated functional application.

**Present operation effective:** 1995-05-15; the component authorities identified above.

**Exceptions and limits:** The reviewed §10A.27(12) covers donations by individuals, political committees and political funds to covered committees or funds; recipients exclude a candidate’s principal campaign committee and a political party unit under §10A.275. The holding creates no general invalidity of candidate limits, higher intermediary limits, coordination rules or demonstrated conduit restrictions.

**Holdings navigation:** This $100 intermediary-contribution ceiling lacks sufficient fit.

## Standards and Tests selection: Nonprofit political spending outside a literal safe harbor

### Nonprofit political spending outside a literal safe harbor

**Governing question:** Independent expenditures by a political nonprofit with incidental business activity and insignificant corporate funding.

**Current rule:** Failure to meet a statutory safe harbor because of incidental business activity or absence of a formal policy against significant corporate contributions does not alone defeat MCFL protection. A voluntary political organization whose resources reflect political support rather than commercial accumulation, whose structure avoids economic claimants and corporate conduits, and whose actual business income and corporate funding are minimal and insignificant may receive as-applied protection. Material commercial accumulation, economic claimants or corporate or union conduit funding requires a different assessment.

**Authority by component:**

- MCCL receives protection on its actual nonprofit characteristics: MCCL receives protection on its actual nonprofit characteristics, 1995-05-15. Stone-Zsela's Opinion of the Court, Part IV, joined by all eight Associates: nine direct votes on this as-applied holding. No general overruling or endorsement beyond Austin's surviving scope is adopted.

**Present operation effective:** 1995-05-15; the component authorities identified above.

**Exceptions and limits:** Section 211B.15(15)’s safe harbor requires no business activity, no economic shareholders or claimants, no establishment by a business corporation or union, and a policy against significant contributions from them. Missing the literal checklist does not itself establish the constitutional regulatory predicate. This does not overrule Austin in its materially different corporate setting, decide direct candidate contributions or immunize future changes in nonprofit operations. Day’s responsive-financing judgment has no controlling five-Justice framework and supplies none of this rule.

**Holdings navigation:** MCCL receives protection on its actual nonprofit characteristics.

## Standards and Tests selection: Independent political-party campaign expression and candidate connections

### Independent political-party campaign expression and candidate connections

**Governing question:** Application of the Senate party-expenditure ceiling and the alternative candidate-contribution theory to a genuinely independent party advertisement.

**Current rule:** Section 441a(d)(3)'s Senate-election expenditure ceiling cannot be applied to a party's own genuinely independent campaign advertisement merely because the speaker is an official political party. Party identity or a continuing electoral relationship also cannot replace §441a(a)(7)(B)(i)'s required cooperation, consultation, concert, request or suggestion by a candidate, authorized political committee or agent for the asserted contribution theory. Actual independence defeats that theory; realistic corruption and circumvention concerns do not alone establish the statutory candidate connection.

**Authority by component:**

- Independent-expression protection: Independent party expression; distinct contribution predicate: The alternative contribution theory, 1996-06-26; O’Connor Part I, joined by Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Breyer (six).

**Present operation effective:** Colorado Republican, 1996-06-26.

**Exceptions and limits:** The general contribution/expenditure distinction survives. Transfers between national, State, district, local and subordinate committees of the same party retain their exemption from §441a(a)(1)–(2); candidate-material republication under §441a(a)(7)(B)(ii) and earmarking or intermediary direction under §441a(a)(8) have different predicates. The rule creates no immunity for candidate cash, genuine conduits, sham independence or coordinated expression.

**Open question:** No majority either validates or invalidates all coordinated party-expression limits or resolves every interaction with §441a(d)(1)’s notwithstanding clause. Neither three-Justice further framework supplies controlling law.

**Holdings navigation:** Colorado Republican Federal Campaign Committee v. Federal Election Commission, 518 U.S. 604 (1996).

## Standards and Tests selection: Candidate financing, political-committee thresholds and membership exclusions

### Candidate financing, political-committee thresholds and membership exclusions

**Governing question:** Whether predominantly issue-oriented groups are exempt from FECA political-committee duties for otherwise covered candidate financing.

**Current rule:** Buckley and MCFL supply no categorical organization-wide major-purpose exemption for genuinely covered candidate financing. Section 431(4)(A) reaches a committee, club, association or other group receiving contributions aggregating over $1,000 in a calendar year or making expenditures aggregating over $1,000 in a calendar year, subject to actual definitions, exclusions and constitutional limits. Establish membership, covered transactions, actual candidate connection and thresholds before imposing duties. Where a contribution theory requires cooperation, consultation, concert, request or suggestion, ideological alignment, lobbying or partisan identity alone is insufficient. Independent expression retains its protection.

**Authority by component:**
- No categorical major-purpose exemption: Akins, Akins v. FEC — III. Major purpose is not a categorical exemption for otherwise covered candidate financing, Souter Part III with Stevens, O'Connor, Ginsburg and Breyer (five for both candidate-cash/conduit and broader covered candidate-financing subparts; Kennedy joins only the former), 1997-06-25.
- Distinct exclusions and reporting conditions: Akins, Akins v. FEC — IV. Membership exclusions and their distinct reporting proviso govern the remand, seven-Justice Part IV, 1997-06-25.

**Present operation effective:** Akins, 1997-06-25.

**Controlling construction:** Section 431(9)(B)(iii) excludes membership-organization or corporate communications to members, stockholders, or executive or administrative personnel when the organization is not primarily organized to influence federal nomination or election. Its separate proviso requires reporting direct costs of communications expressly advocating a clearly identified candidate's election or defeat when costs exceed $2,000 per election, except communications primarily about other subjects, under §434(a)(4)(A)(i) and, for a general election, (ii). Section 441b(b)(2) separately excludes corporate communications on any subject to stockholders and executive or administrative personnel and their families, and labor communications to members and their families; its nonpartisan registration/get-out-the-vote exclusion covers those respective recipients. Its separate-fund exclusion covers establishment, administration and solicitation for a political separate segregated fund by a corporation, labor or membership organization, cooperative or corporation without capital stock. Its loan exception concerns ordinary-course national or State bank loans under banking law and regulations. Sections 431(8)(B)(vi) and (9)(B)(v) cross-reference activity allowed by §441b without importing the $2,000 proviso.

**Open question:** Particular organizational or donor-disclosure burdens retain supported constitutional challenges. The construction supplies no automatic membership, transaction, threshold or liability finding.

**Holdings navigation:** Akins v. FEC (1997-06-25) — III. Major purpose is not a categorical exemption for otherwise covered candidate financing; Akins v. FEC (1997-06-25) — IV. Membership exclusions and their distinct reporting proviso govern the remand.

## Standards and Tests selection: Concrete electoral-information injury

### Concrete electoral-information injury

**Governing question:** Whether voters seeking particular campaign-finance information still withheld have Article III standing.

**Current rule:** Denial of particular information allegedly required by FECA sought for a voter's own electoral participation is a concrete injury even if widely shared. When an erroneous legal premise blocks a disclosure-capable process, possible later lawful agency discretion does not defeat traceability or redressability. Complainant status or a general desire for legal enforcement alone does not suffice. Ordinary standing elements still require stage-appropriate proof, and standing does not establish that the information is legally owed.

**Authority by component:**
- Continuing information deprivation, traceability and redressability: Akins, Akins v. FEC — I. The continuing denial of particular electoral information is a concrete injury, Souter with Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Ginsburg and Breyer (seven), 1997-06-25.

**Present operation effective:** Akins, 1997-06-25.

## Standards and Tests selection: Anonymous individual political leaflets

### Anonymous individual political leaflets

**Governing question:** Compelled identification on an individual’s independently produced political issue leaflets.

**Current rule:** A content-defined demand that an individual identify herself on ordinary political issue leaflets burdens core political speech, including anonymity, and requires exacting scrutiny: narrow tailoring to an overriding state interest. Viewpoint neutrality or the election setting does not lower scrutiny. General source-evaluation interests do not justify a name-and-residence-or-business-address mandate on truthful independent individual leaflets; fraud prevention requires a narrowly fitted connection rather than categorical identification of such advocacy.

**Authority by component:**

- Compelled identification on these political leaflets requires exacting scrutiny: Compelled identification on these political leaflets requires exacting scrutiny, 1995-04-19. Justice Stevens's opinion of the Court, joined in full by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer: seven direct rationale votes. Justice Thomas concurs only in the judgment on his distinct anonymous-political-pamphlet ground; Justice Scalia dissents.
- The asserted voter-information interest does not justify this identification demand: The asserted voter-information interest does not justify this identification demand, 1995-04-19. Justice Stevens's opinion of the Court, joined in full by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer: seven direct rationale votes. Justice Thomas concurs only in the judgment on his distinct anonymous-political-pamphlet ground; Justice Scalia dissents.
- Fraud prevention does not justify this application to truthful independent advocacy: Fraud prevention does not justify this application to truthful independent advocacy, 1995-04-19. Justice Stevens's opinion of the Court, joined in full by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer: seven direct rationale votes. Justice Thomas concurs only in the judgment on his distinct anonymous-political-pamphlet ground; Justice Scalia dissents.

**Present operation effective:** 1995-04-19; the component authorities identified above.

**Open question:** Candidate finance, committees, coordinated expenditures, large contributions and organizational spending remain distinct. Fraud, impersonation and appropriately tailored disclosure restrictions remain regulable. No universal personal-correspondence or small-item exemption is created.

**Holdings navigation:** Compelled identification on these political leaflets requires exacting scrutiny; The asserted voter-information interest does not justify this identification demand; Fraud prevention does not justify this application to truthful independent advocacy.

## Standards and Tests selection: Civil RICO limitation, new injury and concealed discovery

### Civil RICO limitation, new injury and concealed discovery

**Governing question:** Whether a later predicate or concealment permits recovery of earlier civil RICO losses after the four-year period.

**Current rule:** A later predicate in the same pattern, including an act injuring someone else, does not renew the four-year limitation period for an already actionable injury. A later wrongful act directly causing a genuinely new injury may support recovery for that injury without reviving older damages. Damages genuinely too speculative or incapable of proof earlier may accrue when they occur; continuing calculable loss, insufficient investigation or a later calculation of old harm does not meet that qualification. Fraudulent-concealment tolling requires the plaintiff to show concealment prevented timely discovery despite reasonable diligence. Misleading conduct alone is insufficient where reasonable inquiry would reveal the claim; extraordinary investigation overcoming otherwise successful concealment is not required.

**Authority by component:**
- No stale-injury revival and distinct new-injury/unprovable-damage routes: Klehr, Klehr v. A.O. Smith Corp. — I. A later predicate does not renew a stale injury and Klehr v. A.O. Smith Corp. — II. New injury and previously unprovable damages are different from continuing loss, Breyer Parts I–II, six direct joins, 1997-06-19.
- Diligence for concealment tolling: Klehr, Klehr v. A.O. Smith Corp. — III. Concealment does not eliminate reasonable diligence, Breyer Part III, eight Associates, 1997-06-19.

**Present operation effective:** Klehr, 1997-06-19.

**Open question:** No universal injury, injury-discovery or injury-and-pattern-discovery accrual trigger is selected. Common product, damage type, defendant or pattern does not conclusively make an injury old; the required direct causal relation remains. The diligence holding is not a rule for every equitable-estoppel doctrine.

**Holdings navigation:** Klehr v. A. O. Smith Corp. (1997-06-19) — Business and Commercial Law / Civil RICO limitations and concealment.

## Standards and Tests selection: Write-in voting within the complete ballot-access system

### Write-in voting within the complete ballot-access system

**Governing question:** Whether a ban on write-in voting violates electoral-choice or independent expressive rights.

**Current rule:** Under the existing Anderson inquiry, the court assesses the character and magnitude of the actual injury against the State's precise interests and the extent to which those interests require the burden. Severe burdens require narrow tailoring to a compelling interest; reasonable, nondiscriminatory burdens ordinarily may be justified by important regulatory interests. When the complete access system imposes only reasonable burdens, a write-in prohibition is presumptively valid and may be sustained by proportionate interests, including primary finality and prevention of evasive candidacies or party raiding. The ballot need not provide an official count and publication of votes for fictional figures or arbitrary protest messages as an independent expressive entitlement.

**Authority by component:**
- Governing inherited framework: Burdick v. Takushi, “1. Review of election regulations follows the actual burden”, June 8, 1992; White, joined by O'Connor, Scalia, Souter and Thomas (five), applying Anderson and the earlier simulated Norman rule.
- Limited-burden write-in presumption: Burdick, “2. Hawaii's complete write-in prohibition is valid in its reasonably accessible system,” June 8, 1992; same five Justices.
- Arbitrary-message claim: Burdick, “3. The ballot need not serve as an official tally of arbitrary political messages,” June 8, 1992; same controlling five-Justice opinion, with all nine agreeing in rejection of that component.

**Present operation effective:** Burdick v. Takushi, June 8, 1992, for the write-in presumption and expressive boundary; the underlying Anderson framework is applied unchanged.

**Exceptions and limits:** No absolute validation of all write-in bans follows. Materially more restrictive access systems may impose severe burdens. The rule does not replace strict scrutiny of content-based campaign restrictions on public sidewalks.

**Holdings navigation:** Burdick v. Takushi, 504 U.S. 428 (1992) — Ballot access and political parties.

## Standards and Tests selection: Presented questions, subsidiary arguments and exceptional Supreme Court review

### Presented questions, subsidiary arguments and exceptional Supreme Court review

**Governing question:** When an issue outside the stated certiorari question may be considered.

**Current rule:** Rule 14.1(a) creates a strong prudential presumption against deciding questions neither stated in the petition nor fairly included, subject to exceptional circumstances. A distinct intervention denial is not fairly included merely because reversing it would permit reaching a settlement-vacatur question; discussion in the petition’s body and merits briefing does not alone suffice. A consistently asserted Teague defense may be subsidiary where it limits application of the very constitutional rule and habeas relief challenged by the petition. Geographic tailoring is fairly included in a challenge to exclusion from designated speech zones. An exceptional extension requires its own supported basis; adversarial briefing, preservation, logical priority or usefulness alone does not enlarge the questions. The duty to notice jurisdictional defects remains separate. A respondent may defend the existing favorable judgment on a record-supported alternative rejected below when doing so neither enlarges its own rights nor reduces the adversary’s rights under that judgment. The Court may also elect to consider a deliberately disavowed legal argument supporting the same preserved claim when it falls within the question presented and can be resolved on the established record without a new factual theory or additional findings. That discretion imposes no duty to consider abandoned grounds and does not erase limits on distinct claims, relief, factual stipulations or missing facts.

**Authority by component:**

- Strong prudential presumption and independent-question boundary: Izumi Seimitsu Kogyo Kabushiki Kaisha v. U.S. Philips Corp — The intervention question was not fairly included and no exception is warranted, 1993-11-30. Per curiam opinion of the Court supported by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, and Ginsburg, seven Justices; Blackmun and Stevens dissent. The reasoned dismissal establishes this question-presentation ruling, not the merits of the judgment below.
- Confined subsidiary Teague defense: Caspari v. Bohlen — The preserved nonretroactivity defense is fairly included here, 1994-02-23. O'Connor's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg; eight Justices. Stevens disagrees with fair inclusion and would decline the defense under Rule 14.1(a).
- Geographic inclusion and independently justified exceptional review: Madsen v. Women's Health Center, Inc — The limited scope of geographic and paragraph (4) review; The independent conduct-language claims remain undecided, 1994-06-30. O'Connor's Part I, joined by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg: eight. Stevens declines these distinct merits questions. O'Connor's Part IV-A, joined by Blackmun, Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg: eight on the Rule 14 ground. Stone-Zsela agrees only in the nonreach disposition for these independently disputed terms and applications and adds no ground.

- The two renewed alternatives may defend the existing favorable judgment: The two renewed alternatives may defend the existing favorable judgment, 1994-11-29. Part II of Ginsburg's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter and Breyer, supplies six direct joins to this reach ruling. Stone-Zsela joins only the dispositions on the two alternatives and adds no reach ground. Scalia and Thomas accept the legal availability of such defenses but do not decide either alternative because their independent ground would sustain the appellate judgment.
- The Court may consider this included legal argument despite its earlier disavowal: The Court may consider this included legal argument despite its earlier disavowal, 1995-02-21. Justice Scalia's reachability portion, joined by Justices Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer. Seven Justices adopt the stated discretionary-review rationale; Chief Justice Stone-Zsela reaches the question but does not join this portion, and Justice O'Connor declines the argument as a prudential matter.

**Present operation effective:** Lebron, February 21, 1995, for the bounded deliberate-disavowal component; X-Citement Video, November 29, 1994, for the favorable-judgment defense; the earlier authorities retain their separate components.

**Exceptions and limits:** Madsen’s separate noise-and-images review rested together on a continuing categorical restraint, direct connection to the clinic remedy, existing medical record, adversarial presentation and severable legal correction. It declined further independent conduct-language questions despite briefing. Those circumstances are not a universal mandatory checklist or permission to review every related clause.
